current_criteria.name: biological_or_contextual_plausibility
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether an answer’s inferred behavior, context, or usage is contextually reasonable given the visual evidence — but ONLY when the answer is already factually consistent with the image and visually grounded. It applies exclusively to descriptions involving living beings (animals/humans) or their actions, or plausible interactions with objects (e.g., ‘a dog lying down’, ‘a child holding a toy’). It does NOT apply to: (1) visually verifiable facts (e.g., object counts, colors, positions); (2) stylized, symbolic, or abstract imagery (e.g., logos, icons, cakes); (3) spatial arrangements unless they imply biological or physical impossibility (e.g., ‘a giraffe in a cage’); (4) non-biological entities (e.g., computers, statues, abstract designs). Annotators must first verify visual grounding and factual consistency — if either is violated, the answer is automatically disqualified from plausibility evaluation. Plausibility is assessed only after these prerequisites are met, and must be based solely on the visual evidence and real-world context — no speculative assumptions are allowed. For example, if the image shows a dog lying down, describing it as ‘relaxed’ is plausible; describing it as ‘singing opera’ is implausible. If visual evidence is ambiguous (e.g., indistinct posture), the answer should remain neutral or descriptive — plausibility judgments should not be made. Plausibility is not a tiebreaker — if one answer is factually incorrect, it is always inferior, regardless of context. It does not penalize specificity or detail if they are visually supported — only evaluates whether the interpretation is reasonable given what is seen. Annotators must avoid using plausibility to justify hallucinations, misidentifications, or unsupported inferences — these are penalized under ‘factual_consistency_with_the_image’ and ‘visual_grounding’. The criterion is inapplicable for non-living subjects, abstract representations, or aesthetic interpretations — those are evaluated under other criteria. When in doubt, prefer the answer that makes the fewest speculative assumptions while remaining factually grounded.

current_criteria.name: completeness
current_criteria.description: Completeness is evaluated ONLY for answers that are factually consistent with the image — any answer containing hallucinations, misidentifications, or factual errors is automatically disqualified from completeness evaluation. Completeness measures whether the answer includes all major, visually verifiable elements that are directly relevant to answering the question’s intent — not every visible detail, but only those whose omission would render the answer incomplete or misleading. Annotators must first verify visual grounding and factual consistency before assessing completeness. If an answer is factually consistent, completeness is judged by whether it covers all essential visual components necessary to fully address the question — including object identity, spatial relationships, actions, or contextual elements (e.g., background objects, accessories, or implied states) that are visually present and semantically necessary. Adding non-essential, hallucinated, or speculative details (e.g., inventing a ‘camel’ or ‘legs bent’ not visible) does not improve completeness — it reduces quality. Omitting clearly visible, relevant visual elements (even if not central to the question’s literal wording) is penalized. Examples: If the question asks ‘What is in the foreground?’, omitting a clearly visible object in the foreground is incomplete; if the question asks ‘What is the person doing?’, omitting visible motion or posture is incomplete. Conversely, adding contextually appropriate, visually grounded details (e.g., describing a visible logo or background color) enhances completeness. Completeness does not apply to aesthetic, subjective, or stylistic descriptions (e.g., ‘messy’ or ‘balanced’) unless they are grounded in observable visual evidence — and even then, they are not required. Completeness is not about verbosity or exhaustive listing — it is about covering only the essential visual components required to fully answer the question. If two answers are factually consistent, the one with more essential, relevant visual elements wins — but only if those elements are visually present and not hallucinated. Completeness is never used to evaluate or override factual consistency — factual consistency is the primary and non-negotiable prerequisite. If an answer is factually inconsistent, it cannot be considered complete, regardless of its detail level. Completeness is evaluated only after factual consistency is confirmed — and only among factually consistent answers. Annotators must reject any answer that contains factual errors for completeness evaluation, and instead evaluate it based on factual consistency first. The criterion does not apply to open-ended, interpretive, or aesthetic questions — in which case, visual grounding and factual consistency are the only evaluation criteria. Completeness should not be used to penalize accurate but non-critical details — e.g., background colors or subtle textures — unless they are essential to answering the question’s intent. If the question does not require object identification or description, then object details are not essential — and omitting them does not constitute incompleteness. The goal is to ensure that factually correct answers are complete in their coverage of the question’s core intent, without over-rewarding detail or penalizing accurate but peripheral descriptions.

current_criteria.name: factual_consistency_with_the_image
current_criteria.description: The answer must align precisely with the visually verifiable elements present in the image — no fabrication, misidentification, omission of clearly visible elements, or misrepresentation of spatial, structural, or visual attributes is permitted. Annotators evaluate whether every claimed visual detail (objects, positions, colors, textures, labels, spatial relationships, and micro-details) is directly supported by what is visibly present. If visual evidence is ambiguous (e.g., blurry text, partially obscured objects), the answer may express calibrated uncertainty (e.g., 'possibly 5 pillows') — but must not fabricate or omit elements that are clearly visible. Omitting visible elements is a factual inconsistency unless explicitly irrelevant to the question. The criterion applies only to observable, static, geometric, or structural visual cues — motion blur, implied motion, or contextual inferences (e.g., 'warehouse from shelves') are not grounds for factual inconsistency if they do not contradict visible structure. Hallucinations include adding nonexistent objects, misidentifying existing ones, or claiming actions not visually supported — even if plausible. Factual consistency does not require pixel-perfect accuracy or exhaustive detail — only that claims match the visual record. Subjective inferences (e.g., 'calm,' 'arrogant') or aesthetic judgments are not hallucinations unless they imply a fabricated visual attribute. Contextual or inferential claims are permitted if visually plausible and do not contradict the image. The criterion does not apply to questions asking for opinions, interpretations, or non-visual metadata (e.g., artist names, titles). When two answers are factually consistent, tiebreakers are applied based on completeness or specificity — but only after factual consistency is confirmed. Annotators must prioritize visual evidence over external knowledge, and must reject any claim that contradicts the visual record, even if it seems 'reasonable.'

current_criteria.name: multimodal_coherence
current_criteria.description: Multimodal coherence evaluates whether the textual answer’s claims are visually consistent with the image — meaning no contradiction, hallucination, or misrepresentation of observable visual elements — and only applies when the answer is factually consistent with the image (i.e., visual grounding is confirmed). Annotators must verify that every stated visual element (object, action, spatial relation, posture, or inferred state) is either directly visible or logically and conservatively inferred from unambiguous visual cues (e.g., posture suggesting motion, context implying tool use). It does NOT apply to: (1) hallucinated or fabricated elements (e.g., ‘using a laptop’ when the person is knitting); (2) subjective interpretations or abstract metaphors (e.g., ‘the cake is shaped like a train’ — if visually supported, it is acceptable, but not if fabricated); (3) cases where visual evidence is ambiguous or insufficient — in which case, calibrated uncertainty should be applied instead of forced inference; (4) non-visual elements (e.g., opinions, emotions, or contextual inferences not tied to visual evidence). When evaluating, annotators must: (a) confirm factual consistency with the image first — if violated, multimodal coherence is irrelevant; (b) check for internal contradictions (e.g., ‘standing on a curved track’ while the image shows a straight path); (c) verify that inferred actions or states are grounded in observable posture, motion, or context (e.g., ‘drinking from a bowl’ is inferable from posture, but ‘browsing Apple web pages’ is hallucinated unless Apple logos are visible); (d) penalize unsupported speculation — even if plausible — and reward only conservative, visually supported inferences. If two answers are factually consistent, the one with fewer contradictions or more conservative inferences is preferred. The criterion does not evaluate linguistic style, completeness, or plausibility — only strict alignment between text and visual evidence. It is not a tiebreaker for hallucinated or denied elements — those are handled by visual_grounding and factual_consistency_with_the_image.

current_criteria.name: specificity
current_criteria.description: Specificity is the measure of how precisely and granularly an answer describes visually verifiable elements in the image — such as object type, color, texture, spatial position, configuration, or contextual details — without introducing hallucinations or factual errors. It is only evaluated when the answer is factually consistent with the image and visually grounded. An answer is more specific if it adds verifiable, observable details that are present and accurately described, even if minor or non-essential to the question. Specificity does not reward detail quantity, subjective interpretation, aesthetic judgment, or invented details — only precision in describing what is visually present. It is inapplicable when visual evidence is ambiguous or insufficient, in which case calibrated uncertainty should be prioritized over forced specificity. Specificity is not a substitute for accuracy — any factual error or hallucination automatically disqualifies the answer from specificity evaluation, regardless of how detailed it appears. When comparing two answers that are equally grounded and factually consistent, the more specific one (with verifiable granular additions) is preferred — but only if the added detail does not misrepresent scale, position, or proportion. Specificity does not apply to claims about objects 'out of frame' or non-observable elements. Hallucinations (e.g., adding non-existent objects, labels, or actions) are always penalized. Specificity rewards verifiable precision — not exaggeration, absolute claims, or linguistic creativity — and must not override visual grounding or factual consistency. Examples: ‘a red sedan with a sunroof parked next to a curb’ (specific, grounded) is better than ‘a red sedan parked’ (less specific, but still grounded). ‘A cat with a golden collar’ (hallucinated, even if detailed) is penalized. ‘A person holding hands with a child’ (visually verifiable) is specific and rewarded, even if the child is not central to the question. ‘A person with an angry expression’ (subjective, not verifiable) is not specific and penalized. Specificity must be evaluated after confirming visual grounding and factual consistency — if either is violated, specificity is irrelevant.

current_criteria.name: temporal_or_action_coherence
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether an answer correctly describes motion, sequence, or timing that is either visually evident or strongly implied by the image — and only applies when the question explicitly involves dynamic elements (e.g., 'What is happening?', 'Is this person moving?', 'What sequence occurred?'). It does NOT apply to static object descriptions, spatial relationships, or non-temporal questions. Annotators must first verify factual consistency and visual grounding; if an answer is factually incorrect or visually unsupported, this criterion is inapplicable and should not be used to penalize or reward. Only when the image contains motion cues (e.g., blur, mid-air posture, motion trails), implied sequence (e.g., objects arranged in temporal order), or time-sensitive context (e.g., a clock, action in progress) can this criterion be applied. It penalizes hallucinated or unsupported dynamic claims — e.g., describing a static person as 'jumping' without motion cues — but does NOT penalize plausible inferences grounded in visual state (e.g., 'a browser window implies browsing'). The criterion is inapplicable to abstract art, static compositions, or when the question is purely about object identification or presence/absence. Workers should avoid inferring motion from posture alone or aesthetic terms (e.g., 'dynamic' or 'gestural') unless explicitly supported by visual motion cues. When in doubt, the answer with stronger visual grounding and factual consistency should win — temporal coherence is never a tiebreaker if answers are equally grounded.

current_criteria.name: visual_grounding
current_criteria.description: Visual grounding evaluates whether an answer strictly and precisely reflects only what is directly, visibly present in the image — including object identity, location, spatial relationships, actions, colors, shapes, textures, and quantifiable features — without inventing, omitting, or misrepresenting visible elements. Annotators must verify each claim against the visual record: if an object is visible, it must be accurately identified and positioned; if an object is absent, it must not be claimed to be present. Visual grounding requires fidelity to observable details — including subtle, partially obscured, or contextually implied elements — and penalizes hallucinations (fabricating non-existent elements) more severely than misidentifications or omissions. Omitting visible elements that are critical to the question’s answer is a grounding error, but omitting non-essential or ambiguous details (e.g., color if indistinct, motion if blurred) is acceptable if it does not misrepresent the image. The criterion does not require maximal detail or completeness — only fidelity to visible elements. It is inapplicable only when the question asks for opinion, interpretation, or subjective judgment — otherwise, visual grounding is always evaluated. Annotators are allowed to make reasonable, non-hallucinated inferences (e.g., ‘browsing a web page’ if a browser is visible) as long as they are contextually supported and visually implied — and must avoid speculative or structural assumptions not directly visible (e.g., inferring motion or implied structure without visual cues). Visual grounding does not penalize unusual, stylized, or symbolic depictions (e.g., ‘bent legs on a statue’) as long as they are visibly accurate. It does not apply to aesthetic, subjective, or interpretive language (e.g., ‘messy’, ‘cold’, ‘intriguing’) unless such terms directly describe a visible property (e.g., ‘icy’, ‘crystalline’ for cold). The criterion is not about minimizing context or avoiding inference — it is about faithful representation of all visible elements, regardless of their perceived importance. Examples: ‘A red car parked on the left’ is grounded; ‘A red car with a black roof’ is grounded if the roof is visible; ‘A red car with a black object on top’ is hallucinated if no such object exists; ‘A blue horse statue with bent legs’ is grounded even if stylized; ‘a tent’ is grounded if the visual evidence supports it; ‘suspended from metal rods’ is preferred over ‘hanging from the ceiling’ if visual support is visible. The criterion explicitly separates hallucination (claiming non-existent elements) from plausible inference (interpreting visible cues) and penalizes only hallucinations — even if they seem plausible. Visual grounding is always applicable for factual visual description tasks — never for subjective or interpretive questions — and must not be conflated with ‘factual consistency’ or ‘avoidance of hallucination’ — which are distinct criteria. Workers must avoid penalizing for minor aesthetic or stylistic details (e.g., sleeve length, dress color) unless they are critical to answering the question or directly contradict the visual record. The criterion does not require literal precision in every detail — e.g., describing a curved track as ‘straight’ may be acceptable if the image’s focus is on a straight section — as long as it does not misrepresent the overall scene or omit critical visible elements. It also does not require enumeration of every visible object — only those directly relevant to answering the question — and must not penalize for omitting non-essential or ambiguous elements. Finally, visual grounding applies to all visually present elements — including fictional characters, stylized imagery, and symbolic objects — as long as they are correctly identified based on the image, and does not penalize accurate descriptions of posture or structure, even if unusual.

current_criteria.name: clarity_of_implied_relationships
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether the answer explicitly or implicitly links visual elements in a way that is unambiguous and logically supported by the image — especially when describing spatial, causal, or functional relationships between objects. For example, if the image shows a person holding a cup, the answer should not ambiguously say 'the person has something in their hand' without specifying the object. Annotators should assess whether implied relationships (e.g., 'the cat is chasing the ball', 'the door is open because the handle is pulled') are grounded in visible evidence and avoid over-speculation. This criterion does not evaluate factual correctness or visual grounding directly — only how clearly relationships are communicated. It is applicable when the question asks about interactions, configurations, or dependencies — e.g., 'What is the relationship between the dog and the ball?', 'Why is the door open?'. If the relationship is visually ambiguous, the answer may use calibrated uncertainty — but if it invents or misrepresents relationships, it fails this criterion.

current_criteria.name: language_coherence_and_fluency
current_criteria.description: This criterion assesses whether the answer’s linguistic structure is grammatically correct, syntactically smooth, and easy to follow — without jarring phrasing, abrupt shifts, or unnatural constructions — even if the content is factually accurate. It focuses on the clarity and flow of the language, not on semantic meaning or visual fidelity. For example, ‘The cat is sitting on a red rug near the window’ is fluent; ‘The cat sitting on a red rug near the window and then the cat jump off’ is less fluent due to awkward phrasing. Annotators should disregard minor grammatical quirks if they do not impede understanding, but penalize convoluted, redundant, or incoherent phrasing that distracts from comprehension. This criterion is especially important for answers that contain multi-part descriptions or complex spatial relationships. It is not applicable to questions that require highly technical or domain-specific language, where stylistic conventions may vary. The goal is to reward answers that are readable and natural to native speakers.

current_criteria.name: absence_of_redundant_or_irrelevant_details
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether the answer includes only necessary, directly relevant visual elements — without adding unnecessary or off-topic details that do not aid in answering the question. Annotators must distinguish between essential information (e.g., object identity, position, color) and extraneous or decorative details (e.g., ‘the background is blurry’, ‘it’s a sunny day’, ‘the image is high resolution’). Redundant details are penalized if they do not add interpretive value, even if they are visually present — e.g., describing the texture of a wall when the question is about object count. Irrelevant details (e.g., describing a person’s clothing in a question about object placement) are also penalized. This criterion is applicable to all questions — especially those with multiple visible elements — and should be evaluated after verifying visual grounding and factual consistency. The goal is to reward concise, focused answers that minimize noise while preserving precision. Annotators should not penalize contextually helpful details unless they are clearly extraneous or misleading.

all_criteria.name: visual_grounding
all_criteria.description: The answer must strictly and precisely reflect only what is visually present in the image — including object identity, location, spatial relationships, actions, colors, shapes, and quantifiable features — without inventing, omitting, or misrepresenting visible elements. Annotators must verify each claim against direct visual evidence: if an object is visible, it must be named correctly and positioned accurately; if an object is absent, it must not be claimed to be present. Visual grounding requires fidelity to observable details, including subtle or partially obscured elements (e.g., numbers, logos, textures), and penalizes both hallucinations (adding non-existent details) and false omissions (omitting visible elements that mislead or contradict the image’s content). It does not require minimalism or abstraction — detailed, accurate descriptions are preferred if they are visually supported. Annotators should avoid speculative inferences or structural assumptions not directly visible (e.g., inferring motion or implied structure without visual cues), and should flag uncertainty when visual evidence is ambiguous. The criterion is inapplicable only when the question asks for opinion, interpretation, or subjective judgment — otherwise, visual grounding is always evaluated. Examples: ‘A red car parked on the left’ is grounded; ‘A red car parked’ is insufficient if the left/right is critical; ‘A red car with a black roof’ is grounded if the roof is visible; ‘A red car with a black object on top’ is hallucinated if no such object exists.

all_criteria.name: factual_consistency_with_the_image
all_criteria.description: The answer must align exactly with the visual evidence present in the image — no fabrication, misrepresentation, or over-interpretation of ambiguous elements is permitted. Annotators must verify that every claimed visual detail (objects, positions, colors, textures, labels, spatial relationships, and even micro-details like facial expressions) is directly supported by what is visibly present. If an element is ambiguous (e.g., blurry text, indistinct object), the answer may express uncertainty (e.g., 'possibly 5 pillows') but must not fabricate or omit details that are clearly visible. Omitting visible elements is a factual inconsistency — even if minor — unless the omission is due to irrelevance to the question. The criterion does not evaluate scientific plausibility, contextual inference (e.g., inferring a warehouse from shelves), or completeness — only direct visual truth. If two answers are factually consistent, tiebreakers may be applied based on completeness or specificity, but only after factual consistency is confirmed. Hallucinations (adding nonexistent objects, numbers, or relationships) are critical errors, while minor omissions or plausible inferences (e.g., 'indoors' from visible windows) are not, as long as they don’t contradict the image. Annotators must compare answers pixel-by-pixel where possible and reject any claim that contradicts the visual record, even if it seems 'reasonable' or 'plausible'.

all_criteria.name: avoidance_of_hallucinated_visual_details
all_criteria.description: The answer must not invent or exaggerate visual details not present in the image. For example, claiming a person is holding a phone when none is visible, or describing a background object that doesn’t exist — such details are considered hallucinations and reduce quality.

all_criteria.name: question_relevance
all_criteria.description: The answer must directly address the question asked. If the question asks about composition, an answer focusing on the animal’s mood is off-topic. Annotators check whether the answer targets the core intent of the question, not tangential or irrelevant information.

all_criteria.name: completeness
all_criteria.description: Completeness refers to whether the answer includes all major, visually verifiable elements directly relevant to answering the question — without hallucinating, fabricating, or omitting key visual components. Annotators evaluate completeness only when the answer is factually consistent with the image (i.e., no hallucinations or factual errors). An answer is incomplete if it omits a clearly visible and relevant visual element necessary to fully answer the question (e.g., failing to mention a dog in a question about animals). Conversely, adding non-essential or hallucinated details (e.g., inventing a ‘camel’ or ‘legs bent’ not visible) does not improve completeness — it reduces quality. Completeness is not about verbosity or listing every object; it is about covering only the essential, observable visual components that directly address the question’s intent. Annotators should prioritize accuracy over detail and ignore non-essential background or speculative context. Completeness must be assessed within the bounds of visual grounding and factual consistency — an answer with factual errors cannot be considered complete, even if it appears comprehensive.

all_criteria.name: specificity
all_criteria.description: Specificity refers to the inclusion of granular, visually grounded details that are directly observable and verifiable in the image — such as object type, color, texture, spatial position, or exact configuration — without introducing hallucinations or factual errors. An answer is more specific if it adds precise visual attributes that are present and identifiable, not speculative or invented elements. Specificity is not rewarded if the added detail contradicts the image or introduces false certainty. It must be evaluated in tandem with factual consistency and visual grounding — if two answers are equally grounded, the more specific one wins only if it does not sacrifice accuracy. Specificity does not mean verbosity or subjective interpretation; it means precision in describing observable features. It is inapplicable when visual evidence is ambiguous or insufficient, in which case calibrated uncertainty should be prioritized over forced specificity. Examples of acceptable specificity: ‘a red sedan with a sunroof parked next to a curb’ (observable details). Examples of penalized specificity: ‘a red sedan with a sunroof parked on a curved track’ (if the track is not visible) or ‘a cat with a golden collar’ (if no collar is visible).

all_criteria.name: calibrated_uncertainty
all_criteria.description: The answer should reflect confidence appropriately. If the image is ambiguous, the answer should indicate uncertainty (e.g., “possibly” or “likely”) without overstating certainty. Annotators penalize overconfidence in uncertain situations and reward humility when appropriate.

all_criteria.name: clear_language
all_criteria.description: The answer should be written in simple, grammatically correct, and unambiguous language. Jargon, overly complex phrasing, or unclear syntax reduce clarity and accessibility. Annotators prefer answers that are easy to understand without requiring interpretation.

all_criteria.name: logical_consistency
all_criteria.description: The answer must be internally coherent and free from contradictions. For example, if it says an animal is both “calm” and “in pain,” or that objects are “on opposite sides” while also “centered,” it lacks logical consistency. Annotators evaluate whether the answer’s internal logic aligns with the visual evidence.

all_criteria.name: biological_or_contextual_plausibility
all_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether the answer’s inferred behavior, context, or interpretation is consistent with real-world knowledge — but ONLY when the visual evidence does not contradict it. It applies exclusively to descriptions involving living beings (animals/humans), their actions, or plausible object usage/interactions. For example, if an image shows a dog lying down, describing it as 'relaxed' is plausible; saying it is 'singing opera' is implausible. The criterion does NOT apply to: (1) visually verifiable facts (e.g., object counts, colors, positions), which are evaluated under ‘factual consistency’; (2) stylized, symbolic, or abstract imagery (e.g., logos, cakes, icons); (3) terminology precision or linguistic correctness; (4) spatial arrangements unless they imply biological or physical impossibility (e.g., ‘giraffes in a cage’). Annotators should prioritize visual grounding and factual consistency first — plausibility is only assessed if those are satisfied. If the answer contains hallucinations or contradicts the image, it is automatically invalid regardless of plausibility. When evaluating plausibility, workers must rely solely on the visual evidence and real-world context, avoiding speculative assumptions. If visual evidence is ambiguous, the answer should remain neutral or descriptive — plausibility judgments should not be made in such cases.

all_criteria.name: multimodal_coherence
all_criteria.description: The answer should seamlessly integrate visual and linguistic information — ensuring that the text does not contradict the image and that any implied actions, states, or objects are visually supported. Annotators evaluate whether the answer maintains consistency between what is seen and what is described, even when abstract or inferential language is used.

all_criteria.name: cultural_or_situational_appropriateness
all_criteria.description: The answer should be contextually appropriate given the cultural, social, or situational setting implied by the image — e.g., whether the description respects norms (e.g., not describing nudity or inappropriate content in non-consensual contexts) or aligns with real-world usage (e.g., not misrepresenting object function). Annotators assess whether the tone, content, and framing are suitable for the image’s implied context.

all_criteria.name: temporal_or_action_coherence
all_criteria.description: The answer should correctly describe dynamic elements (e.g., motion, sequence, or timing) if visible or implied in the image. For example, if the image shows a person mid-jump, the answer should not describe them standing still. Annotators check whether the description aligns with implied motion, sequence, or duration — especially for action or time-sensitive questions.

manager_prompt:
List and describe 10 criteria for how human annotators compare the quality of two answers to the same visual question.

The task is RLHF-V style preference comparison for visual question answering and image-text responses. The worker model will receive:
- the image,
- the source question,
- candidate answer A,
- candidate answer B.

Focus on human preference factors such as visual grounding, question relevance, factual consistency with the image, avoidance of hallucinated visual details, completeness, specificity, calibrated uncertainty, and clear language.
